what: Paired aft trim-ballast reservation under the auxiliary room: 2 m3 each. Curved outboard faces follow the hull minus 0.10 m geometric clearance; centreline gap 0.40 m; floor is at least 0.10 m above the loft. Gross 5.3916 m3, 4.8524 m3 after a provisional 10% structure allowance. This replaces the former tank outside the stern hull without crowding the fuel tanks.
why: Trim ballast; final framing and net tank calibration remain to be engineered

what: Steering-gear room: two rudder stocks, rams and tie bar; two 2.2 kW hydraulic power units; the emergency hand pump; the rudder-angle transmitter; the stern-tube oil header tanks; the 5.5 kW emergency fire pump with its own sea suction; a sound-powered telephone and the emergency steering notice
why: Steering, and a fire pump outside the engine room

what: Fresh-water tanks port and starboard, 6 m³ each, the stern tubes between them
why: Water for the taps, the galley and the toilets: 1.5 m³ a day

what: Engine room (batch 6c: from z 8.5, where the counter leaves room for floor plates): the two main engines (x ±1.55, z 9.6–12.0) with their gearboxes aft and turbochargers forward, the shafts aft through the bulkhead; the forward service band of the main engines extends to z 14.0; the two generators are in the auxiliary room; the control booth aft to starboard; fire and general-service pumps, bilge pump, sanitary pump, hydrophore set along the starboard side; the starting-air compressor and two 150 L air bottles against the aft bulkhead to port; the workbench, the fuel purifier and the oily-water separator along the port side; the 1.5 m3 fuel service tank in the forward starboard corner; the sea chests under the plates either side forward; CO₂ nozzles overhead; the watertight door forward on the centreline to the auxiliary machinery room
why: Propulsion and power. Low: 1.9 m clear, and tall men duck under the pipes

what: Engine control booth (2.3 × 1.6 m, soundproofed, glazed towards the engines): the main switchboard on the aft bulkhead, the engine panel and the log desk along her side, the telephone to the bridge
why: Where the chief engineer stands his watch out of the noise

what: Double bottom under the engine room: fuel storage port and starboard (7.5 m3 each), bilge holding (1 m3), sludge (0.3 m3), lubricating oil (0.6 m3): total 16.9 m3 against 18.5526 m3 planning envelope after a 10% structure allowance. Individual tank partitions and calibration remain to be designed.
why: Fuel storage: calculated 9.23 days at the stated duty and 90% usable capacity, excluding idle and weather allowance

what: Shaft space aft of the engine room, over the counter: the two shafts from the gearboxes to the stern tubes, the fresh-water tanks’ fill and air pipes
why: The hull rises aft of z 10.5; the shafts run through here at a slope
unmanned: Reached through a manhole in the engine room’s aft bulkhead, for the shafts’ couplings

what: Auxiliary machinery room, through the watertight sliding door at Fr 28 (kept shut at sea, slid by its hand pump at the door or closed from the bridge): two generator sets relocated to z15.20-16.05 with a 1.00 m centre aisle and at least 1.035 m to side plant; the ballast and bilge manifold and the ballast pump along the starboard side over the tanks they serve, the sewage holding tank (4 m³) and its two discharge pumps to port with the standby pumps in a row before them (fuel transfer No.1 and No.2, hydrophore No.2, sanitary No.2), starting-air compressor No.2 in the aft starboard corner, the sounding pipes to the double bottom, the escape trunk in the forward starboard corner up into casing S
why: The hold forward of the engines was 13.5 m of tanks and voids; a yard puts the auxiliaries that want no watch here, out of the noise, with the ballast valves over their tanks

what: Workshop, through the door at Fr 38: the bench and vice along the forward bulkhead, the JL-400 centre lathe along her side, the pedestal drill, the bench grinder, the welding set, the tool board; a wiped main-bearing shell on the bench, kept for the surveyor
why: Repairs alongside at a bench with room to swing a hammer: the engine room has only the small bench by the ladder

what: Engine store, behind the mesh partition off the workshop: the spares racks (filters, gaskets and seals, injectors, bearings, belts, lamps), two 200 L lubricating-oil drums on their rack with a drip tray, the oily-rag bin, a chain block
why: Spares locked away from the car deck, next to the bench that fits them
unmanned: A store: entered to fetch a part; its one door is the workshop’s, a step from the aux room

what: Double bottom under the auxiliary room, workshop and store: paired trim tanks 2 m3 each at z14.1-15.4; main ballast port and starboard 8 m3 each at z15.6-20.0. These disjoint conformal reservations have 4.8524 and 16.4238 m3 respective planning envelopes after a 10% structure allowance. Unassigned reserve is not additional certified capacity.
why: Heel and trim, with capacities and framing subject to tank design

what: Void between the store and the thruster room: the thruster’s cable and the fore peak’s ballast line run through it; a manhole in the store’s forward bulkhead
why: Kept as a reserve: the ferry office talked of a cold store for the island’s fish and never ordered it

what: Bow-thruster room: the 75 kW motor on its 0.9 m tunnel, the starter cabinet
why: Berthing: it pushes the bow off and on
unmanned: Nobody works in it at sea: it is visited alongside, with the thruster isolated, through its one hatch

what: Fore peak: 6 m³ of ballast, and the two chain lockers under the windlasses
why: Trim, and the anchors’ cables

what: Aft mooring station: the 5.5 kW capstan, two pairs of bitts, closed fairleads, the steering-gear hatch
why: Stern lines

what: Lower lobby (batch 6f), the car deck’s level aft of the lanes, between the casings under a 2.5 m deckhead: the drivers’ waiting benches along the casings, the bicycle rack and the baggage shelf either side of the crew door in the aft bulkhead, a drink machine and the safety plan on the forward bulkhead, lifejacket lockers; the engine-room door (casing P) and its escape (casing S), the feet of both passenger stairs, the foyer from the gangway, the crew door aft to the mooring station, and two 1.1 m sliding fire doors forward onto the lanes
why: Where the drivers wait, the islanders’ bicycles ride, and every way below and above begins: the ways are found, not hunted for

what: Vehicle lanes, 17.4 m: two of 2.75 m, yellow lane lines and numbers, 24 cloverleaf lashing sockets on a 1.25 × 2.5 m grid, wheel-chock racks, six scuppers a side with flaps and freeing ports forward, waterproof tube lights, two exhaust fans, four hydrants, powder extinguishers; the signs “engine off” and “no entry to the car deck at sea”
why: Six cars; a truck on the centreline forward by the loading plan

what: Casing, port, 1.3 m wide: the engine uptake and engine-room supply-fan trunk (z 3–6.25), the engine-room entrance (6.3–7.4, a 1.1 m door) and ladder, passenger stair P (7.4–11.3, 1.2 m clear: its 1.2 m door onto the car deck at 11.35–12.55, the flight rising aft at 48° to the lobby, the crew changing room under it), the foyer at its foot (11.3–13.3) and the gangway passage (13.3–14.7, 1.4 m) with the gangway door and the shore-power box, a fan and a hydrant
why: The engine room’s main way in, a stair up for drivers, and the way aboard from the pier

what: Casing, starboard, 1.3 m wide: uptake trunk (z 3–6), the engine-room escape trunk (6–7), passenger stair S (7.4–12.6, 1.2 m clear, its 1.2 m door at 11.35–12.55; the bosun’s store under its flight: lashings, chocks, ropes, fenders), a fan and a hydrant
why: The engine room’s second way out, the deck stores, the second stair up

what: The way aboard on foot, 1.4 m wide the whole way: the gangway, the gate, the passage through casing P and the foyer aft of it to the foot of stair P, 2.2 m under its deckhead
why: Foot passengers never step onto a car lane

what: Bow house, port: the windlass, the ramp’s hydraulic power pack and its control box, the thruster room’s hatch
why: Anchors and the ramp, worked by the bosun

what: Bow house, starboard: the windlass and the paint store
why: Anchors, and paint kept away from the cabins

what: The bow ramp: hinged at the stem (z 34.3), 4.0 m and a 2.0 m flap that lies flat on the landing, 4.4 m clear; two 100 mm hydraulic cylinders at 14 MPa; two locking pins with limit switches to the “ramp closed and locked” lamp on the bridge; a hand pump
why: Lowered, 5° to the quay; raised, it closes the bow 4 m high

what: Open deck: benches for 22 under an awning, one liferaft (port, aft), the rescue boat and its davit (starboard, aft), the stern flagstaff, two lifebuoys, the sign for muster station B
why: Fresh air, the view, and where people embark the liferafts

what: Lobby, the deckhouse’s full breadth: the stair heads P and S in its wings; the purser’s window (S: ticket rack, cash box, punch, PA microphone, first-aid kit, lost property); the kiosk (P counter); the vending corner (two drink machines and a hot-water dispenser for cup noodles); timetable and fare boards; the capacity sign and the ship’s certificate; an ashtray stand by the aft door
why: Tickets and snacks; everyone passes through

what: Toilets: men’s to port (a WC, two urinals, a basin), women’s to starboard (two WCs, a basin); sea-water flushing
Carpet room, raised 0.3 m: carpet, a rack of cushions and blankets, the shoe shelf at the step, a television on a bracket, life-jacket lockers; 36 places
why: Lie down for twenty-two minutes, as everyone does

what: Seated saloon: a cross passage at its aft end to the side doors (z 16.5–17.6), then 42 moquette seats in seven rows of three each side at 0.85 m, windows forward over the car deck and the sea, life-jacket lockers, the sign for muster station A
why: The forward view

what: Side walkway, port, 0.7 m: rails, two liferafts in cradles outboard of the rail, a hydrant, and the ladder up to the bridge wing at its forward end (z 17.6–19.5)
why: Crew and escape

what: Side walkway, starboard, 0.7 m: rails, two liferafts in cradles outboard of the rail, a hydrant, and the ladder up to the bridge wing at its forward end (z 17.6–19.5)
why: Crew and escape

what: Emergency-generator room: the 40 kVA emergency generator, the emergency switchboard, the 24 V batteries and their chargers, a 60 L day tank, louvres
why: Power when the main board is dead; its door opens to the open deck only

what: CO₂ room and fire-control station: four 45 kg CO₂ bottles, the release cabinet, the remote fan stops and fuel quick-closing valves, two firemen’s outfits
why: Fire in the engine room is fought from outside it; its door opens to the open deck only

what: Crew cabin, two berths: the bosun and the oiler; bunk beds, lockers, a fold-down desk
Chief officer’s cabin
Deckhand’s cabin
why: On her weeks aboard

what: Crew WC and shower
Mess room: a table for six, a television, a kettle, the duty board and the muster list
why: Where the crew eat and the watch is handed over

what: Galley: a three-plate range, the rice cooker, a fridge-freezer, a sink, a hood, the provision locker, a hatch to the mess
why: The cook’s; the kiosk’s hot water too

what: Chief engineer’s cabin
Master’s cabin: a desk, a bunk, the ship’s papers and the safe
The crew’s corridor down the middle, from their own door aft onto the bridge deck’s platform (they come up the open deck’s ladders) to the wheelhouse
why: The crew’s way to their rooms and to the bridge, apart from the passengers

what: Wheelhouse: the steering stand (wheel, non-follow-up lever, autopilot); two engine levers and the thruster lever at the centre and on both wing consoles; the radar; the magnetic compass periscope; VHF with DSC; the ship’s telephone; the NAVTEX printer; the echo sounder; the GPS display; the chart table with its drawers and red lamp; the navigation-light panel; the fire panel; the PA and general alarm; the ramp lamps; the whistle button; the searchlight control; the wipers; a clock, a barometer, an inclinometer; the log desk; the master’s high chair
why: She is conned from here and from the wings

what: Bridge wing, port, open: a wing console with the engine and thruster levers, the port sidelight at its end
why: Berthing port side to

what: Bridge wing, starboard, open: a wing console, the starboard sidelight at its end, the float-free EPIRB
why: Berthing starboard side to

what: Compass deck: the standard magnetic compass, the mast with the radar scanner on its platform, the masthead light at 15 m, the all-round lights, the whistle, the VHF and GPS antennas, the searchlight, the company flag
why: What she sees and is seen by

what: Funnel, port: the port main engine’s and No.1 generator’s exhausts
why: Twin funnels at the open deck’s forward corners, clear of the bridge-deck house

what: Funnel, starboard: the starboard main engine’s and No.2 generator’s exhausts
